notes: Lord Woolf on second default-judgment set-aside application and Enron misrepresentation pleading; agency analysis is detailed.

enrichment.short_title: Enron v Clapp: default judgment, issue estoppel and fraudulent misrepresentation
key_facts: Enron group companies sued individual shareholders of TBNG under a share charge securing liabilities under a Turkish gas joint venture agreement.
Default judgments for about US$8.1 million were partly set aside by Langley J, leaving about US$3.9 million outstanding on quantum and set-off grounds.
After that hearing the defendants sought to set aside the balance and plead fraudulent misrepresentation about Enron's financial strength to induce entry into the JVAs and charge.
The defendants had not pleaded misrepresentation at the original set-aside hearing despite earlier awareness of a fraud-in-the-inducement case.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Applications to strike out a late misrepresentation defence and to set aside the remaining default judgment after Langley J's partial set-aside order, with a pending Court of Appeal.
enrichment.outcome: No jurisdiction to entertain a second High Court application to set aside the balance of the default judgment; misrepresentation defence struck out as having no real prospect of success, though not barred by issue estoppel or abuse of process as a damages/set-off defence.
enrichment.ratio: A perfected default judgment affirmed on the merits cannot generally be reopened by a second set-aside application where fresh defences were available earlier; damages for misrepresentation may be pleaded without impugning contract validity, but a corporate principal is not liable for continuing group representations unless employees or Enron Corp were clothed with actual or apparent authority from the contracting entities.
legal_issues: Whether the court could hear a second application under CPR Part 13.3 to set aside the balance of a default judgment
Whether issue estoppel or abuse of process barred a misrepresentation defence to the upheld judgment sum
Whether Enron Corp became agent of ECT/ETEP so as to fix them with fraudulent financial representations
Whether the proposed pleading had any real prospect of success on agency and vicarious liability
linked_authorities: Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 1

confidence.notes: Four numbered conclusions and detailed procedural reasoning are clearly stated.

notes: Short consequential judgment on permission, costs and interim payment after will validity appeal; limited substantive ratio.

enrichment.short_title: Sherrington v Sherrington: consequential costs after will execution appeal
key_facts: Claimant children challenged the due execution of their father's will; the widow Yvonne succeeded on appeal and took the whole estate.
The Court of Appeal refused permission to appeal further to the House of Lords.
The litigation was described as very hostile, with serious allegations against the successful appellant.
The court urged the widow to consider mercy before enforcing substantial costs orders against the testator's devoted children.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Consequential applications after the Court of Appeal allowed the defendant's appeal on will validity, addressing permission to appeal, costs and an interim payment.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused; appellant awarded full appeal costs; claimants ordered to pay 50% of trial costs; administrator and administration costs to be paid from the estate; interim payment of £50,000 ordered.
enrichment.ratio: Where an appellant succeeds in substance on appeal, the ordinary costs rule applies to the whole appeal costs; at trial, reasonable litigation of due execution can justify only partial recovery of the successful party's costs in hostile family will disputes.
legal_issues: Whether permission to appeal should be granted
Apportionment of appeal and trial costs between successful appellant and unsuccessful claimants
Whether claimants' costs should be paid from the estate
Appropriate interim payment on account of appeal costs

confidence.notes: Orders are explicit though the underlying merits decision is not restated.

notes: Leading equal pay preliminary issue on indirect discrimination statistics in Prison Service HEO comparator case.

enrichment.short_title: Home Office v Bailey: equal pay and prima facie indirect sex discrimination
key_facts: Nearly 2,000 Prison Service administrative employees claimed equal pay with predominantly male comparator grades such as governors and principal officers.
Lead claimants Clemens and Pollak were Higher Executive Officers whose work was rated equivalent to male comparators but paid less.
Employment tribunal statistics showed women in the disadvantaged HEO group at about 51% versus men at about 9%, a ratio of about 6:1.
The EAT held no objective justification was required because the disadvantaged group was gender-neutral, reversing the tribunal.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal on a preliminary issue whether the Home Office had to objectively justify less favourable terms after work was rated equivalent.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; tribunal decision restored; a prima facie case of indirect sex discrimination was established from gender-composition statistics, shifting the burden to the employer to justify the pay disparity.
enrichment.ratio: Where pay differs between occupational groups and statistics show a significantly higher proportion of women than men in the disadvantaged group, the Seymour-Smith/Barry ratio approach may establish prima facie indirect discrimination even without a formal requirement or condition; section 1(3) then requires the employer to prove a genuine material factor unrelated to sex.
legal_issues: Whether indirect discrimination required identification of a requirement or condition
Whether Enderby-type group comparison or Seymour-Smith statistical analysis applied
Whether a gender-neutral disadvantaged group precluded prima facie discrimination
Who bore the burden of proving disparate impact
linked_authorities: Glasgow City Council v Marshall [2000] ICR 196
Enderby v Frenchay Health Authority [1994] ICR 112
Barry v Midland Bank plc [1999] ICR 859

confidence.notes: Detailed analysis of statutory scheme and ECJ guidance with clear appellate restoration of the tribunal.

notes: Landmark guidance on Criminal Justice Act 2003 bad character gateways; three applications refused.

enrichment.short_title: R v Hanson: admissibility of defendant bad character under CJA 2003
key_facts: Three linked applications raised how trial judges should admit evidence of a defendant's previous convictions under the new bad character regime.
Section 101(1)(d) permits admission where bad character is relevant to an important matter in issue, including propensity to commit the offence or to be untruthful.
Hanson pleaded guilty to theft after burglary convictions were ruled admissible; Gilmore and Pickstone unsuccessfully challenged similar rulings.
The court emphasised applications should not be routine and each prior conviction must be analysed individually.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Full Court guidance and determination of three Crown Court leave applications on admissibility of previous convictions under the Criminal Justice Act 2003 bad character provisions.
enrichment.outcome: General guidance given; Hanson's, Gilmore's and Pickstone's applications for leave to appeal against conviction were refused as convictions were safe.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 101(1)(d) and section 103 the judge must ask whether convictions establish propensity, whether that propensity makes guilt more likely, and whether admission would be unjust or unfair; propensity to untruthfulness is distinct from dishonesty and usually requires disbelieved account or false representation, with strong jury directions against undue reliance.
legal_issues: Construction of section 101 gateways for previous convictions
When same-description convictions show propensity to commit the charged offence
Distinction between propensity to dishonesty and propensity to untruthfulness
Notice requirements and fairness under sections 101(3) and 103(3)
linked_authorities: R v Makanjuola (1995) 2 Cr App R 469
R v Chalkley and Jeffries [1998] 2 Cr App R 79

confidence.notes: Authoritative procedural guidance and disposal of three applications are comprehensively reasoned.

notes: Waste exemption construction for woodchip manufacture; appeal dismissed on both Paragraph 13 and 21 grounds.

enrichment.short_title: Environment Agency v Armstrong: exempt wood waste storage and chipping
key_facts: Armstrong Environmental was convicted of knowingly depositing controlled timber waste on Link 25 land without a waste management licence.
The company intended to chip painted and varnished wood for animal bedding, fuel or chipboard manufacture; less than 1,000 tonnes were stored.
The Crown Court held the activity exempt under Schedule 3 paragraph 13 as manufacture of timber products from waste wood.
The Environment Agency appealed by case stated, arguing woodchip was not a timber product and the waste was not waste plant matter under paragraph 21.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated against a Crown Court decision allowing Armstrong's appeal and holding the deposit fell within exempt activities under the 1994 Regulations.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; reducing waste wood to woodchips was manufacture of timber products under paragraph 13, but paragraph 21 did not apply because the material was waste wood rather than waste plant matter.
enrichment.ratio: On a natural reading of paragraph 13, manufacture from waste wood includes producing woodchips as a timber product even if not a finished good; paragraph 21 covers chipping of waste plant matter such as bark, not processed waste wood already falling within paragraph 13.
legal_issues: Whether woodchips are timber products for paragraph 13 exemption purposes
Whether manufacture includes an intermediate processing stage rather than only finished goods
Whether deposited timber waste qualified as waste plant matter under paragraph 21
Burden of proving exemption on the defendant under section 101 MCA 1980
linked_authorities: Environment Agency v M.E. Foley Contractors Ltd [2002] 1 WLR 1754

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and split outcome on two exemption paragraphs are clearly explained.

notes: Costs appeal on several guarantees; Chadwick LJ restores 100% indemnity costs against each guarantor.

enrichment.short_title: Venture Finance v Mead: several guarantors and indemnity costs orders
key_facts: Venture Finance sued two directors for about £530,804 under separate deeds of guarantee and indemnity supporting an invoice discounting facility to SLC.
Each guarantee capped principal liability at £100,000 but clause 9 required payment of all recovery costs on a full indemnity basis.
The parties settled on £92,500 plus interest from each guarantor but disputed whether each was liable for 100% or 50% of proceedings costs.
Beatson J ordered each defendant to pay 50% of indemnity costs, treating several liability as necessarily splitting the costs bill equally.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a costs order made after compromise of summary judgment proceedings without trial of the substantive quantum and cap issues.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; each guarantor ordered to pay the whole of the claimant's costs of the proceedings, with contribution as between guarantors limited to one half each; judge's 50% order set aside.
enrichment.ratio: Several liability under separate guarantees does not automatically limit each guarantor to half the claimant's costs; clause 9 indemnified all costs arising out of recovery under each guarantee, and virtually all costs were common to both defendants so 100% was recoverable from each subject to no double recovery in aggregate.
legal_issues: Whether a judge should determine costs after compromise without tried substantive issues
Effect of several as opposed to joint and several liability on costs
Whether CPR 48.3 or CPR 44.3 governed allocation of costs between parties
Construction of an indemnity costs clause in separate guarantee deeds
linked_authorities: BCT Software Solutions Ltd v C Brewer & Sons Ltd [2004] FSR 9

confidence.notes: Detailed costs reasoning with clear corrective order, though one guarantor was bankrupt.

notes: SENDIST jurisdiction appeal; no second appeal against tribunal-amended SEN statement.

enrichment.short_title: Dean v East Sussex: SENDIST jurisdiction over tribunal-amended statements
key_facts: Twin girls with special educational needs appealed a statement naming A school; the tribunal amended Parts 2 and 3 by agreement but upheld A school in Part 4.
After attending A school the parents sought a further tribunal appeal against the amended statement, citing changed circumstances.
Jack J held section 326(1)(b) did not permit appeal against a statement amended pursuant to a tribunal order under section 326(3)(b).
The parents' out-of-time review application under regulation 37 had been refused and no extension was sought.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Administrative Court on whether the SENDIST had jurisdiction to hear a second appeal against a statement amended to give effect to an earlier tribunal order.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; no right of appeal to the tribunal against a statement amended pursuant to the tribunal's own section 326(3)(b) order; regulation 37 review was the appropriate route for post-decision changed circumstances.
enrichment.ratio: Parliament cannot sensibly have intended a second tribunal appeal against a statement the tribunal itself ordered the LEA to amend; section 326(2)(a) expressly excludes similar appeals after paragraph 11(3)(b) orders, and changed circumstances after a final decision should be pursued by review under regulation 37, potentially with extended time in the interests of justice.
legal_issues: Whether section 326(1)(b) covers statements amended under section 326(3)(b)
Construction of section 326(2) exclusions for tribunal-ordered amendments
Whether a second appeal was vexatious where Parts 2 and 3 had been agreed
Alternative remedies by review, reassessment or annual review
linked_authorities: R v Clwyd County Council ex parte A [1994] 1 FCR 334
White v Aldridge and London Borough of Ealing [1999] ELR 150

confidence.notes: Statutory scheme and purposive construction are carefully reasoned, with obiter on vexation.

notes: TPO challenge failed after committee reconsidered with colour photograph; seal witnessing point rejected.

enrichment.short_title: Aspdin v Derby: tree preservation order and procedural fairness
key_facts: Derby City Council made and confirmed a TPO protecting a pine tree at 27 Penny Long Lane on visual amenity grounds.
Claimant executor Aspdin objected, supplying a colour aerial photograph said to show the tree lacked public prominence.
At the first confirmation meeting members received only a poor black and white copy, not the agreed colour photograph.
The committee later reconsidered with the colour photograph displayed and confirmed the order; Aspdin also challenged seal witnessing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Section 288 challenge to making and confirmation of a tree preservation order after planning committee proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; failure to circulate the colour photograph at the first meeting did not cause substantial prejudice after full reconsideration; presumption of regularity defeated the seal witnessing challenge.
enrichment.ratio: Where an objector expressly relies on a colour photograph as integral to representations and the council agrees to provide it, failure to do so is a procedural defect; but if the committee fairly reconsiders with the photograph and reaches the same conclusion, quashing would not restore a different outcome and discretion should refuse relief.
legal_issues: Whether Regulation 5 required proper consideration of objections including the colour photograph
Whether procedural unfairness caused substantial prejudice warranting quashing
Effect of subsequent committee reconsideration curing the defect
Whether witnessing signatories proved the corporate seal was properly affixed

confidence.notes: Fact-sensitive procedural fairness analysis with clear dismissal on both grounds.

notes: Urgent contempt appeal; Channel 5 Gangsters broadcast allowed despite murder investigation sensitivity.

enrichment.short_title: Greater Manchester Police v Channel 5: contempt and broadcast restraint
key_facts: Desmond Noonan was murdered in Manchester and a suspect was arrested but not yet charged.
Channel 5 planned to broadcast a programme entitled Gangsters featuring the Noonan family's violence and witness intimidation.
The Chief Constable obtained an injunction restraining broadcast on the ground of risk to witness cooperation.
Extensive local and national publicity about the killing and the Noonan family had already appeared.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Urgent application for permission to appeal and appeal against Poole J's same-day order restraining broadcast of a television programme during an active murder investigation.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal granted; appeal allowed; injunction quashed; broadcast restraint not justified on the high section 2(2) test.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 2(2) the applicant must satisfy a high standard that publication would create a substantial risk of serious prejudice to active proceedings; general notoriety of witness intimidation and existing publicity mean a dramatic programme does not necessarily add enough incremental risk, especially where jury prejudice is not the primary concern.
legal_issues: Whether section 2(2) was engaged by an active arrest without charge
Standard of proof for pre-publication contempt injunctions
Risk to potential witnesses as opposed to jurors
Whether the programme materially increased existing intimidation risk
linked_authorities: Attorney-General v MGM Ltd [1997] 1 All ER 459

confidence.notes: Short extempore appellate judgment with clear application of the strict contempt test.

notes: Major patent entitlement and abuse-of-process judgment in Markem v Zipher thermal printer dispute.

enrichment.short_title: Markem v Zipher: patent entitlement and abuse of confidence strike-out
key_facts: Markem and Zipher disputed entitlement to thermal printer patents after former Markem employees developed the Zodiac machine at Zipher.
In entitlement proceedings Markem did not allege breach of confidence or other wrongdoing, relying only on section 7 invention ownership.
HHJ Fysh held mixed entitlement and granted cross-licences; the Court of Appeal reversed on the thermal printer group.
Markem later brought a separate breach of confidence action which the judge refused to strike out; the Court of Appeal held that was an abuse.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals and cross-appeals from patent entitlement judgments and appeal from refusal to strike out a subsequent breach of confidence claim.
enrichment.outcome: Zipher's entitlement appeal allowed and cross-appeals dismissed; separate breach of confidence claims struck out as abuse of process under Johnson v Gore Wood principles.
enrichment.ratio: Section 7 alone cannot found a section 8 entitlement claim without showing the patentee lacked title through breach of contract, confidence or similar rule of law; wide claims developed at Zipher from McNestry's ideas owed nothing to Markem's non-confidential wish-lists; keeping confidence claims in reserve after entitlement proceedings harasses defendants and is abusive.
legal_issues: Whether section 7 creates freestanding entitlement under section 8
Whether Markem materials such as Adkin, Windsor and CCL memoranda supported entitlement
Appropriate claim-by-claim versus information-use analysis under section 8
Whether later breach of confidence proceedings were an abuse of process
linked_authorities: Johnson v Gore Wood & Co [2002] 2 AC 1
Markem Corpn v Zipher Ltd (No 1) [2004] RPC 233

confidence.notes: Long reported judgment with numbered conclusions on entitlement and abuse clearly stated.
